{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01C5Ji6vuFEM1G4Kf8K2oFxq","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). They add risk/security and organizational\n116\t  dependencies, such as a business associate agreement before patient data reaches a new\n117\t  vendor, and the skeleton still runs in production on a designated test record.\n118\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"bb59a773-8b66-4f69-994c-212aa570633a","uuid":"d50ed48d-824d-4439-b987-4f31bf70a383","timestamp":"2026-10-02T23:58:33.044Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p140aff59\\skills\\dependency-first-architect\\reference\\validation.md","content":"# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n\nExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_br5o6lthx2f5mybzvuphqxzuon5iuy34rqml3gbevdqtlpxmwjca","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Real-time collaborative document editor\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A browser-based rich-text editor. Several users edit the same document at once, see each other's changes live, and every document is saved permanently.\n- **Type:** Software, greenfield, not a small build. It has outside users, user content that may include personal data, and several R3 decisions (merge model, saved format, who-can-access-what).\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness. Every copy of a document must end up identical, and no edit the user was told is saved may be lost.\n- **Worst failure:** An edit shown as \"Saved\" disappears, or copies silently drift apart and corrupt the document. A close second is a user opening a document they are not allowed to see. V3 and V5 guard these two.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Remote edit delay (a keystroke on A appears on B, same region) | p95 < 200 ms, p99 < 500 ms | ASSUMPTION: a commonly cited point where edits feel live; product owner to confirm | V0 records the floor; V4 |\n| Local typing delay | p95 < 16 ms from key press to screen, on a 1 MB document | ASSUMPTION: one frame at 60 Hz | V1 |\n| Document open time | p95 < 1.5 s for a 1 MB, ~200-page document with a year of edit history | ASSUMPTION: a large but realistic document | V1 |\n| Simultaneous editors per document | 50 | ASSUMPTION: similar products cap live editors at around 100; product owner to confirm | V4 |\n| Total simultaneous connections | — | UNKNOWN: needs the launch user forecast from the product owner before Phase 4 sizing | V4 sizing, Phase 5 |\n| RPO for saved edits | 0 confirmed edits lost | ASSUMPTION: users treat \"Saved\" as a promise; product owner to confirm | V3 |\n| RTO | Collaboration server back in < 1 min (clients keep editing locally meanwhile); full database restore < 1 h | ASSUMPTION: starting values to confirm | V3 |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the uptime the business will commit to, from the product owner, before Phase 5 opens to everyone | V7 |\n| Storage | Bytes stored per document ≤ 3× its latest snapshot, after compaction | ASSUMPTION: keeps the edit log from growing without limit | Phase 2 exit |\n| Operational complexity | 2 deployable services + Postgres (Redis only after V4); one on-call rotation | ASSUMPTION: one team of 4–8 people | Phase 4 exit |\n\n**Missing inputs.** The phase order rests on four assumptions:\n- **We run it as a hosted service in the browser.** If it ships for customers to install themselves, Phase 0 becomes an installable release, and upgrade and version-compatibility gates move up.\n- **It is a rich-text editor.** If it is plain text or code, V2 shrinks a lot.\n- **Offline-first editing is not required.** If it is, browser-side storage and long-offline merge tests move into Phase 1 and V1, and content stored on devices joins V6.\n- **No regulated content (health, payments).** If there is, those obligations become dependencies that block real content in Phase 2.\n\nNumbers still needed: the scale forecast, the SLO, any data-residency requirement, and team size.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Saved-format design and any lasting document | V1 (the merge library converges and is fast enough) | validation / decision | specified |\n| Editor features (tables, images, comments, history) | V2 (old and new app versions can safely edit the same document) | validation | specified |\n| Real content in documents (internal use) and edit-log compaction deletes | V3 (durability) | risk/security | exposed (deletes: committed) |\n| Any outside user, and link sharing | V5 (access control), V6 (privacy) | risk/security | exposed |\n| Privacy review, data-processing agreements with vendors (cloud, login provider, error tracker) | Legal/privacy owner. Starts in Phase 0 because of lead time | organizational | exposed (Phase 5) |\n| External security test | Vendor booked in Phase 1 | organizational | V5 → exposed |\n| Production cloud account, domain, login-provider (OIDC) tenant | Account owner | organizational | built (Phase 0) |\n| Multi-server collaboration design and beta limits on editors per document | V4, plus the scale forecast | validation | specified / scaled |\n| Opening to everyone | SLO input, a staffed on-call rotation, V7 | organizational | committed |\n\nNo economic dependency binds before launch: no money changes hands. Hosting cost per connection is recorded at the Phase 4 exit.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| How concurrent edits merge (consistency vs availability) | R3: the saved format and sync protocol depend on it; once real documents exist, switching means converting every document | Merge-by-design shared data type (CRDT: Yjs + y-prosemirror). Every client edits locally and all copies converge. The server relays and saves edits but does not decide between them | Yjs converges for this schema and is fast enough at the target document size | V1 | V1 fails, or the product needs the server to reject individual edits → server-ordered edits instead (OT: ShareDB + prosemirror-collab) |\n| When \"Saved\" is shown | R3: a lost confirmed edit cannot be undone | The server writes the edit to the Postgres edit log before confirming it. Peers receive the edit right away. The client keeps and resends anything not yet confirmed | One commit per edit batch fits the remote-delay budget | V3 (no loss), V4 (delay) | Confirmation delay p95 over budget → batch commits in 50 ms windows. Never confirm before the write |\n| Document schema and saved format | R3: every stored document is in this shape | Minimal ProseMirror schema v1 (paragraphs, headings, lists, bold/italic/link). Every snapshot is stamped with its schema and format version. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Request:** An allow-listed staff member signs in, creates a document, and types \"hello\". A second browser session sees it. A synthetic check every 5 minutes opens a test document in two clients, types, and confirms the edit arrives.\n- **Rolled back:** Redeploy the previous image through the pipeline. Database migrations only add, never remove. Clients reconnect with backoff.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only staff in a login-provider group, behind a feature flag. Documents are **disposable test data**: a banner says so, and wiping is allowed until V3 passes, because the saved format is not yet validated.\n- **Exit check (V0):** One traced request succeeds across every tier. A deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline. Killing the database connection fires the save-failure alert. A deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline. Killing the database connection fires the save-failure alert. The first values for remote delay, save delay and document open time are recorded as baselines.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Convergence, document model, identity**\n  - **Unlocks:** Committing to the saved format and the schema-evolution path.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 0, V0.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Run the V1 test harness and benchmark.\n    2. Settle the IDs and workspace-ID columns.\n    3. Write the permission tables and the connection-time check as a decided contract (owner/editor only for now).\n    4. Freeze schema v1 and its version stamp.\n    5. Set limits on edit message size and rate per connection.\n    6. Add a client-version check at connect.\n    7. Run V2.\n    8. Book the external security test vendor.\n  - **Rollback:** Data is still disposable. Revert and wipe.\n  - **Exit check:** V1 and V2 pass. The drift detector (below) is live in the skeleton.\n\n- **Phase 2: Durability and sync protocol**\n  - **Unlocks:** Staff use the editor for real content (internal use is the first exposure, the smallest group).\n  - **Depends on:** V1, V2.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Save before confirming, and have clients resend unconfirmed edits.\n    2. On reconnect, sync only what each side is missing (Yjs state vectors).\n    3. Turn on point-in-time recovery and encrypted backups.\n    4. Script a restore drill.\n    5. Compact the edit log into snapshots: decode each snapshot and compare it with a replay of the log before deleting log entries, then keep the log for 30 more days.\n    6. Run V3.\n  - **Point of no return:** Ending the wipe policy, and the first deletion of compacted log entries. Both are guarded by V3.\n  - **Exit check:** V3 passes. The storage-per-document ratio stays within budget on documents in internal use.\n\n- **Phase 3: Access control, sharing, privacy**\n  - **Unlocks:** Being ready for outside users.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 2. The privacy review and vendor agreements started in Phase 0.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Full roles, checked on every edit.\n    2. Workspace membership.\n    3. Revocation that disconnects live sessions.\n    4. Link sharing (off by default).\n    5. Audit log of permission changes.\n    6. Sanitize pasted HTML (the schema strips unknown markup; block `javascript:` links); strict content-security policy.\n    7. Run V5 (automated test matrix, then the external test) and V6.\n  - **Rollback:** Feature flags per capability. A permission-schema change is reversed with the add-then-remove migration pattern.\n  - **Exit check:** V5 and V6 pass.\n\n- **Phase 4: Collaboration-server scale and editor features**\n  - **Unlocks:** Beta limits and sizing; editor features.\n  - **Depends on:** V2 (for features), V3, and the scale forecast (for sizing).\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Run V4.\n    2. Add Redis multi-server sharing, or route each document to one server if V4 calls for it.\n    3. Drain connections smoothly on deploy.\n    4. Cap editors per document and slow down senders who flood it.\n    5. Then the lower-risk features, each one schema-evolved through the V2 suite:\n       - live cursors and presence (temporary, never saved)\n       - tables\n       - images: upload through pre-signed links, check file type and size, serve from a separate sandboxed domain\n       - version-history view built from the snapshots\n  - **Rollback:** Every feature behind a flag. Multi-server mode can fall back to a single server.\n  - **Exit check:** V4 passes. The on-call load review is done. Hosting cost per 1,000 connections is recorded.\n\n- **Phase 5: Outside exposure, smallest first**\n  - **Unlocks:** Opening to everyone (general availability).\n  - **Depends on:** V5, V6, V4. The SLO input and a staffed on-call rotation.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. One allow-listed outside workspace, capped at the V4 editor limit.\n    2. Widen to 5, then 25 workspaces, then open signup. Each step waits for 7 days of SLO data with no lost-edit or drift alerts.\n    3. Run V7.\n  - **Rollback:** Turn off the cohort flag. Existing documents stay readable and exportable.\n  - **Exit check:** V7 passes.\n\n## 6. Deliberately deferred\n- **Offline-first editing (browser storage):** pull forward if product requires it, or if telemetry shows many sessions offline for more than 5 minutes. It then extends V1 and V6.\n- **Comments and suggestion mode:** pull forward when product prioritizes it. Each goes through the V2 suite.\n- **Full-text search (fed from the outbox):** pull forward when workspaces reach more documents than browsing can handle, by product signal.\n- **Import and export (.docx, PDF):** pull forward on customer demand. An open-format export (JSON/Markdown) comes first if the build-vs-buy decision flips.\n- **End-to-end encryption:** pull forward on enterprise demand.
